assigned.title: A CI step that hangs reports 'in progress' for six hours instead of failing
assigned.acceptance:
REQUIRED: the jobs in ci.yml and windows.yml get `timeout-minutes`, per step where a step has a credible hang and per job otherwise. THE CLASS, NOT THE INSTANCE. PL-0735 fixes the one step that hangs today; this makes the NEXT one visible. A step with no bound burns GitHub's six-hour default and reports 'in progress' the entire time -- indistinguishable, to the only readable channel this project has (annotations, because job logs need a login), from a runner that is merely queued. That is how CI #181 and #182 both sat unfinished without anyone treating it as a failure.

REQUIRED: each bound is derived from an OBSERVED duration and the derivation is written beside it. A number somebody felt was generous is a number somebody will raise the first time it fires. Observed today: e2e 5m 8s, e2e-typecheck 12s, and the Windows e2e-desktop job 3m 25s.

REQUIRED: the bound is not so tight that a slow runner reads as a defect. A timeout that fires on a cold cache teaches people to re-run rather than to read, which costs more than the hang.

OUT OF SCOPE: the control-plane performance work, which is PL-0735, and any change to what the steps do.
assigned.notes:
SPLIT OUT OF PL-0735 in round 112, carrying its clause verbatim. PL-0735 was filed holding ci.yml and `ai:claim` refused it on an overlap with PL-0728, which is in REVIEW for the rest of the round. Keeping both halves in one task meant neither landed; this one is BACKLOG until ci.yml frees.

Classification C (workflow/harness defect) under the round-112 directive's A-E scheme, same as PL-0735. P1 rather than P0 because PL-0735 removes the hang that exists; this prevents the one that does not exist yet.

assigned.title: Every msiexec call in the lifecycle harness can wait forever
assigned.acceptance:
FOUND BY PL-0736 WHILE BOUNDING THE STEP THAT CONTAINS IT. `lifecycle.mjs` calls `spawnSync("msiexec.exe", args, { encoding: "utf8", windowsHide: true })` four times -- install, upgrade, uninstall, reinstall -- and passes no `timeout`. Windows Installer serialises on the `_MSIExecute` mutex and a holder makes the next invocation WAIT rather than fail, so there is no deadline anywhere in the chain that decides F1, F3 and F4.

PL-0736 put a 15-minute `timeout-minutes` on the step. That is an OUTER bound and deliberately not the fix: when it fires, the whole step dies and the report says nothing about which case stalled or why.

REQUIRED: a `timeout` on each msiexec invocation, and a timed-out case REPORTED as a case outcome with its own reason, not collapsed into a crash. The harness already distinguishes exit 1 (a real case failure) from exit 2 (a refusal over arguments or platform) precisely so a configuration mistake is not filed as a product defect; a stall is a third thing and must not be filed as either.

REQUIRED: the bound is per-invocation and derived. A silent install of this MSI is seconds of work.

REQUIRED: a timed-out case is NEVER recorded as pass, and never as not-run with a reason that reads like a deliberate skip -- F2's `not-run` means 'the evidence does not exist', and a stall means 'we did not find out'.

OUT OF SCOPE: changing what any case does, and the step-level bound PL-0736 added, which stays as the outer limit.
assigned.notes: P2 rather than P1 because the outer bound now exists, so the failure mode is 'the step dies at 15 minutes with a poor message' rather than 'the job burns an hour'. It is still a real defect: the message is what a person reads at 2am.

unit.evidence:
node --test scripts/windows/test-lifecycle.mjs: 42 tests, 42 pass (was 33; this task adds 9). Full npm run test:scripts: green, rc=0. repo:validate: passed.

TWO CASES RUN A REAL CHILD RATHER THAN ASSERTING A BELIEF ABOUT spawnSync. The whole repair rests on Node's timeout semantics, so they are exercised: a child that sleeps 60s with timeout 250 returns status null and error.code ETIMEDOUT; a missing binary returns status null and error.code ENOENT. THAT PAIR IS THE DEFECT -- the old code tested status !== 0, so a stall and an absent msiexec.exe both arrived as a bare fail with status: null and nothing to read.

MUTATION-TESTED, five ways this repair could be undone:
  no-timeout        (delete timeout from the spawn options)   -> 1 test fails
  stall-is-notrun   (a stall recorded as not-run)             -> 2 tests fail
  gate-off          (jobFailed returns false)                 -> 2 tests fail
  spawn-as-stall    (a spawn failure dressed as a timeout)    -> 1 test fails
  timeout-too-long  (180s -> 300s)                            -> 1 test fails

The first and last are the ones worth naming. no-timeout is the mutant every other case in this block would survive, because they drive classifyInvocation with synthetic results and would keep passing while timedOut quietly never became true again on a machine nobody in this container can run; it is caught only because the spawn options are a frozen exported value with an assertion on them. timeout-too-long is caught because the step bound arithmetic is ASSERTED rather than left in a comment: four invocations at 300s is 20 minutes against PL-0736's 15-minute timeout-minutes, so the step would die with no report and the deadline would have bought nothing.

NOT CLAIMED: nothing here runs msiexec, and no Windows machine was involved. What is tested is the decision -- what an invocation means -- which is the same division the rest of this harness keeps between residue.mjs deciding and msiexec measuring.

assigned.title: desktop-shell-ci.yml is the one workflow with no timeout at all
assigned.acceptance:
FOUND BY PL-0736, OUTSIDE ITS SURFACE. That task's acceptance names `ci.yml` and `windows.yml` and its allowedPaths hold exactly those two, so this file was not touched -- but the audit that produced the bounds read every workflow, and `windows-shell` is now the only job in this repository with no `timeout-minutes`, job-level or step-level.

Its shape is the one most likely to stall: `dtolnay/rust-toolchain`, a Swatinem cache restore, and `cargo test`/`clippy`/`build --release` on a Windows runner, all of which reach the network and the first of which is the single slowest minute this repository spends.

REQUIRED: a job bound derived from an observed duration, with the derivation written beside it, in the same form `ci.yml` now uses.

REQUIRED: generous. A Windows Rust release build on a cold cache is genuinely long, and a bound that fires on one teaches people to re-run rather than to read.

OUT OF SCOPE: anything the job does, and the new `experiment-1a.yml`, which was written with `timeout-minutes: 45` already on it.
assigned.notes: P3 because this job is not on the release path -- `windows.yml` is what produces installers -- and because a six-hour stall here is visible as an unfinished run rather than as a wrong answer. Recorded now so it is written down rather than remembered.

assigned.title: The installed MSI never starts its sidecar, and the splash spins forever instead of saying so
assigned.acceptance:
THE SYMPTOM, FROM THE COMMANDER'S INSTALLED MSI: the window shows "PROJECT LIBERTY -- Starting... -- Preparing the local service" indefinitely. His captured log shows bundled node.exe being launched and then dying with: Error: EISDIR: illegal operation on a directory, lstat 'C:', at Object.realpathSync, at Function._findPath, at resolveMainPath. So node starts and cannot resolve the main script it was given.

WHAT IS PROVEN FROM CODE, AND WHAT IS NOT. Proven: Node's resolveMainPath calls Module._findPath, which for the main module calls toRealPath -> fs.realpathSync on the resolved request; realpathSync splits the root with the regex /^(?:[a-zA-Z]:|[\\/]{2}[^\\/]+[\\/][^\\/]+)?[\\/]*/ (read out of the installed node binary, not from memory) and lstats that root on Windows. Proven: plan_launch builds both paths with Path::join against constants that contain FORWARD SLASHES -- "sidecar/node.exe" and "sidecar/server/liberty-sidecar.js" -- so the joined path has mixed separators. NOT proven: which of those produced the literal string 'C:' in the error. The pasted log shows backslashes where the constants have forward slashes, so separator detail has been normalised out of the transcript and the exact bytes Node received are not recoverable from it. An attempt to read the real log file was made and the folder-access request went unanswered.

REQUIRED: THE PATHS HANDED TO NODE ARE PLAIN AND PLATFORM-SEPARATED. Two independent defects are fixed rather than one guessed at, because each is wrong on its own terms. (a) A relative path written with forward slashes must be joined COMPONENT BY COMPONENT so the platform separator is used; under a Windows extended-length prefix the OS does not translate a forward slash at all, which Microsoft documents, so a mixed-separator path is not merely untidy. (b) Any \\?\ extended-length prefix must be removed before the path reaches Node, because Node's own module resolver reasons about Windows roots with the regex above rather than through the Win32 path parser.

REQUIRED: THE UNC FORM IS LEFT ALONE. \\?\UNC\server\share is NOT stripped: the correct plain form is \\server\share and a naive prefix removal would produce a path that silently addresses something else. Only the drive-letter form \\?\X: is normalised, and the UNC case is tested.

REQUIRED: THE COST OF STRIPPING IS STATED RATHER THAN HIDDEN. The extended-length prefix exists to escape MAX_PATH. Removing it reintroduces that limit for these paths. That is accepted because Node cannot consume the prefixed form at all, so the alternative is not a longer path but no launch; and the MSI's own install location is far under the limit. It is recorded in the source so a future reader does not rediscover it as a surprise.

REQUIRED: THE LAUNCH LOG RECORDS THE ARGUMENTS, NOT JUST THE EXECUTABLE. The host currently logs only launch.node, which is why this round could not establish what Node actually received. It must log the full argument vector and the resolved paths. The token is provably not among the arguments -- launch_arguments returns one element and the_token_never_reaches_the_spawn_arguments asserts it -- and that property must be re-asserted now that the argv is written to a file a person will paste.

REQUIRED: A STARTUP FAILURE IS VISIBLE WITHOUT DEPENDING ON A LISTENER THAT MAY NOT EXIST YET. apps/desktop/dist/index.html registers its handler with `await listen("liberty://startup-failure", ...)`. That await resolves asynchronously, and a sidecar that dies in milliseconds reaches surface_failure before it does. Tauri does not replay events, so the failure is emitted into nothing and the splash spins forever -- which is exactly what the commander saw, and it means the supervision machinery worked and the report was lost. The failure must reach the page whether or not a listener is registered at the moment it happens.

REQUIRED: THE REGRESSION TEST SPAWNS A REAL NODE. A mocked ShellHost cannot catch this class of defect: every existing ordering test passed while the installed application could not start. The test must run the actual node executable against a script at an installed-style path CONTAINING SPACES, and assert it executes. On Windows it must additionally construct the extended-length form and demonstrate the difference between the raw and normalised paths, so the fix is pinned to observed behaviour rather than to a reading of documentation.

MUST NOT: weaken sidecar authentication, the loopback bind, the handshake's host refusal, origin or Host-header validation, the request guard, or the token's absence from argv. None of those is implicated and none may be touched to make a path problem go away.

MUST NOT: leak the token into the log, into the argv, into a path, or into any user-visible failure text. The log gains the argument vector this round, which makes that property load-bearing rather than incidental.

MUST NOT: claim the installed application works. CI can establish that node resolves a script at a spaced installed-style path and that the shell's ordering and failure handling hold. It cannot establish that the MSI starts, that the handshake completes on a real machine, or that the UI renders. That is the commander's MSI test and it is the only thing that can close this.
assigned.notes: FILED 2026-10-11 from the commander's captured installed-MSI startup log. Round 127 fixed a 403 that stopped the webview loading its own page; this is the defect behind it -- the sidecar it would have loaded from never starts. Both were invisible to every gate this project has recorded, for the same reason: the shell has only ever been exercised through a mocked host, and PW-0504 is BLOCKED. The real-node test required here is the first test in this repository that runs the actual runtime against an installed-style path.

build.evidence:
BUILD: cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -D warnings clean for x86_64-pc-windows-msvc AND the host. Cargo.lock unchanged. repo:validate passed. UNIT: cargo test --locked, 76 passed, 0 failed (73 before this correction, 3 added).

THIS GATE REPLACES THE ONE RECORDED AGAINST b3d410d, WHICH PASSED CODE WHOSE WINDOWS-ONLY TEST COULD NOT RUN. Windows CI run 38109614525: 72 passed, 1 failed, sidecar::real_node::node_is_given_the_plain_path_and_not_the_extended_length_one.

THE DEFECT IS IN THE TEST FIXTURE, NOT IN THE PRODUCTION CODE, and the distinction is the finding. src/sidecar.rs:524 read format!(r"\?\{}", server.display()) -- a THREE-character prefix. An extended-length prefix is four characters: backslash, backslash, question mark, backslash. So the fixture built a near-miss that is not an extended-length path at all; without_extended_length_prefix correctly declined to strip it and returned the path unchanged; and the assertion failed. The function did exactly what it was written to do, and the conservative behaviour it showed is the same one a_unc_extended_length_path_is_left_exactly_as_it_arrived asserts deliberately.

THE CONSEQUENCE, WHICH IS THE PART THAT MATTERED: the Windows behaviour of round 128's fix was UNPROVEN. The single assertion meant to establish it never tested a real prefix, so a green Linux run plus a red Windows run together established nothing about whether a real \\?\C:\... path gets normalised. Round 128's claim to have fixed the launch path was therefore weaker than its gate evidence implied, and that is on me rather than on CI.

CAUSE, STATED PLAINLY AND IT IS MINE TWICE IN ONE ROUND. The Rust source was generated through Python heredocs and backslash escaping collapsed the literal. The same thing happened to EXTENDED_LENGTH_PREFIX itself earlier in round 128 -- caught there only because a Linux test exercised it -- and I did not then go back and audit the other literals written in the same batch. An audit now finds exactly one remaining instance (the fixture) and none in windows_host.rs, which has no backslash literals at all.

THE REMEDY IS STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN A CAREFUL RETYPE, because a careful retype is what failed twice.
  1. The fixture now builds the prefixed path FROM EXTENDED_LENGTH_PREFIX. Test and production share one source of truth, so a mangled fixture is impossible by construction.
  2. the_extended_length_prefix_is_exactly_four_characters pins the constant WITHOUT writing another escaped literal: it asserts chars().count() == 4 and compares against characters named through char::from_u32(0x5C) and char::from_u32(0x3F). Nothing in that assertion can be collapsed by whatever writes the file. It runs on every platform.
  3. the_constant_built_prefix_is_the_one_the_function_strips closes the hole that let this escape to Windows CI at all. The drive test typed its own prefix; the Windows-only test built one from the constant; nothing joined them, so the two could disagree and only windows-latest would find out. This builds the input from the constant plus a Windows-shaped drive tail and asserts the whole chain -- constant, prefix recognition, drive check, strip -- on EVERY platform. It also asserts the input was four characters longer than the tail, so a constant collapsed to nothing could not make it pass vacuously.
  4. a_near_miss_prefix_is_not_treated_as_an_extended_length_path pins the shapes that break: the three-character form this fixture produced, a form with no separator after the question mark, one with an extra leading backslash, and one with none. Each must be left untouched.

WHAT I COULD VERIFY WITHOUT WINDOWS, AND WHAT I COULD NOT. I temporarily removed the #[cfg(windows)] gate and ran the real-node test here. It failed -- correctly -- with left "\\?\/tmp/liberty sidecar test .../..." against right "/tmp/...": the constant now contributes a real four-character prefix, and the function correctly refuses to strip it because /tmp is not a drive-letter path. That run proves the constant is right and proves the function's drive check is doing its job, and it proves the test can only run where a drive letter exists. The gate was restored immediately. What remains genuinely unverifiable here is the other half of that test -- whether the real Node then accepts the normalised Windows path -- and point 3 above is why that is now the only unverified part rather than the whole assertion.

THREE MUTANTS, ALL CAUGHT, and the first is the exact mistake this round repairs: removing a backslash from the constant (round 128's own first mangling); adding one; and making the function strip any four leading characters without checking for a drive letter. All reverted, 76/76 green.

NOTHING IN THE PRODUCTION PATH CHANGED. join_relative, without_extended_length_prefix, plan_launch, the argv logging and surface_failure's eval delivery are byte-identical to b3d410d. This round changes one fixture line and adds three tests. No security boundary was near it: no change to the loopback bind, the handshake's host refusal, the token's minting or its absence from argv, the request guard, Host-header validation, or PL-0753's interceptor.

NOT CLAIMED: that the installed MSI starts. What this round earns is narrower and worth stating exactly -- that the path normalisation round 128 introduced is now tested rather than asserted, on both platforms, with the Windows-specific remainder reduced to "does real Node accept it". It does not establish that the MSI starts, that the handshake completes, that the webview loads, or that the UI renders. PL-0753's fix has still never run. PW-0504 is still BLOCKED and is still the only thing that can close any of this.

unit.evidence: cargo test --locked: 76 passed, 0 failed (73 before). Three added: the_extended_length_prefix_is_exactly_four_characters (escape-proof, asserts the constant via char::from_u32 and a length rather than another literal); the_constant_built_prefix_is_the_one_the_function_strips (builds the input FROM the constant and asserts the whole strip chain on every platform -- this is the test whose absence let a three-character fixture reach Windows CI); a_near_miss_prefix_is_not_treated_as_an_extended_length_path (the four shapes that must be left alone, including the exact one the broken fixture produced). The Windows-only real-node test now builds its prefix from the constant too. Three mutants run, all caught, including removing a backslash from the constant. The full diagnosis -- that this was a fixture defect and not a production defect, and what that cost in terms of unproven Windows behaviour -- is in the build gate on this task.

assigned.title: The installed application answers Internal Server Error: the packaged tree points at the build machine
assigned.acceptance:
THE SYMPTOM, FROM THE COMMANDER'S INSTALLED MSI AT f60f2fa. The bundled node.exe launches, the handshake completes -- liberty-sidecar-ready {"host":"127.0.0.1","port":65150} -- and the application then displays Internal Server Error. The captured stderr: Error: Failed to load external module pg-587764f78a6c7a9c / Error [ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND] / Imported from: C:\\Program Files\\Project Liberty\\sidecar\\server\\dist\\desktop\\server\\chunks\\ssr\\[turbopack]_runtime.js. So rounds 127-129 all worked: the sidecar starts, the handshake lands, and the webview is reaching the server. What fails is one module resolution inside it.

THE ROOT CAUSE, ESTABLISHED FROM THE BUILD OUTPUT AND REPRODUCED LOCALLY, AND IT IS NOT A MISSING DEPENDENCY. Next 16.3.1 builds the desktop target with Turbopack. Turbopack externalises some server packages and emits a BARE import of a hashed alias for each: the shipped chunk [root-of-the-server]__0vd44rx._.js contains await a.y("pg-587764f78a6c7a9c"), and [turbopack]_runtime.js's externalImport does await import(id) with that string. Next materialises the alias as a RELATIVE SYMLINK in the build output: dist/desktop/node_modules/pg-587764f78a6c7a9c -> ../../../../../node_modules/pg, which inside the standalone tree resolves to standalone/node_modules/pg. package-sidecar.mjs then copied that tree with fs.cpSync, whose behaviour for a symlink is to resolve the link against its SOURCE directory and write an ABSOLUTE link at the destination (demonstrated in isolation on node v22.22.2: a relative link ../../target became an absolute path into the source tree). The packaged tree therefore shipped server/dist/desktop/node_modules/pg-587764f78a6c7a9c pointing at a directory on the GitHub runner. On the installed machine that path does not exist.

COPYING pg IS NOT THE FIX, AND THE COMMANDER WAS RIGHT TO SAY SO. pg and all nine of its transitive dependencies are already traced into standalone/node_modules by Next's file tracing and already copied to sidecar/server/node_modules/pg by this script. Nothing is missing from the installer. A POINTER leaves the tree. Adding a second copy of pg would have made the symptom disappear while leaving every future externalised package -- and every other symlink any build ever emits -- to fail the same way.

WHY NOTHING CAUGHT IT, which is what the remedy has to answer. sidecar-bootstrap/acceptance.mjs already starts the packaged sidecar and already asserts GET / -> 200. It passes, because on the build machine that absolute link RESOLVES. A tree that is only wrong RELATIVE TO BEING MOVED cannot be caught by any check that does not move it, and no check in this repository moves it. That is the class, and it is wider than this bug: it is every way a packaged artifact can depend on the machine that produced it.

REQUIRED: NOTHING IN THE PACKAGED TREE RESOLVES OUTSIDE IT. The external aliases are materialised into real directories of real files -- what an installer can carry -- rather than repaired as links, because a repaired link still has to survive WiX, an MSI, and whatever a future Windows does about symlinks, and a real file survives all three by not being a question. Materialisation runs to a FIXED POINT with a stated pass budget, because materialising one link can introduce others.

REQUIRED: THE FLAG IS NOT TRUSTED, THE RESULT IS ASSERTED. cpSync's dereference: true option selects the stat applied to the copy ROOT; a symlink NESTED in the tree is still copied as a link. Measured, not assumed: with dereference: true the destination's lstat().isSymbolicLink() is still true on node v22.22.2. Packaging therefore ends with an independent walk of the produced tree that refuses any symlink which does not resolve inside it, dangling ones included.

REQUIRED: A SMOKE TEST THAT MOVES THE TREE. apps/desktop/scripts/packaged-server-smoke.mjs copies the packaged sidecar to a directory outside the repository and, from there: asserts symlink containment; extracts every external specifier from every shipped chunk at its Turbopack call site and resolves each one with Node's own resolver from the chunk that imports it -- the acceptance criterion 'no unresolved external imports', asserted rather than reasoned about; starts the sidecar; and requires 200 from /api/health and from an authenticated / that is an HTML document. The extraction carries non-vacuity floors so a pattern that stops matching fails instead of reporting a clean tree.

REQUIRED: IT RUNS WHERE THE INSTALLER IS BUILT. package-sidecar.mjs invokes it, in the manner it already invokes collect-notices.mjs and for the reason stated there -- the thing that knows what was packaged is the thing that packaged it. windows.yml's package job already runs this script, so the guard executes on the job that produces the MSI with no workflow edit; .github/workflows/{ci,windows}.yml are reserved by PL-0736 this round and were not available to write. It is NOT optional, and the cost is stated: a flake means no installer. For three rounds this project produced installers that could not start, every one from a green job.

MUST NOT: weaken the sidecar's authentication, the loopback bind, the handshake's host refusal, origin or Host-header validation, the request guard, or the token's absence from argv. None is implicated. The smoke test authenticates the way the shell does, with the token header and a matching Host, because a probe that bypassed the guard would be testing a different server.

MUST NOT: add a dependency, change next.config.ts, change what is externalised, or decide whether a desktop build should carry a Postgres driver at all. That last question is real and is referred to gpt-architect rather than answered here: the desktop sidecar now ships pg and has no database, the homepage's import graph reaches it, and with the import resolvable the page renders 200 without one. Removing it is an architecture change, not a packaging fix.

MUST NOT: claim the installed MSI works. What this task earns is that the packaged tree no longer depends on the machine that built it, proven by serving an authenticated homepage from a relocated copy with the entire build output removed from the filesystem. Whether the MSI installs, starts, and renders on the commander's hardware is PW-0504 and remains the only thing that can close it.

=====================================================================
ROUND 130A CORRECTION, FOLDED INTO THIS TASK RATHER THAN FILED BESIDE IT.
=====================================================================

A separate PL-0758 was drafted for the correction below and then withdrawn: the control plane refused it for overlapping this task's reserved paths, and the refusal was right about more than paths. This task's own acceptance says the packaged runtime must have no unresolved external imports and that a Windows packaged-server smoke test must catch this class of failure. The Windows job cannot produce the tree at all, so that acceptance is UNMET and this is the same deliverable continuing -- reopened with ai:start from REVIEW, which preserves implementationBaseSha, rather than reviewed as finished and corrected under a second id.

THE SYMPTOM. Round 130A (b0f22cf) passed CI and the desktop shell and FAILED the Windows package job at the step "Lay out the packaged sidecar" (run 38149713649). The script's own refusal, verbatim:

  package-sidecar: the build output at standalone/apps\\web links OUT of the standalone tree:
  D:\\a\\project-liberty\\project-liberty\\apps\\web\\dist\\desktop\\standalone\\apps\\web\\dist\\desktop\\node_modules\\pg-587764f78a6c7a9c
  -> D:\\a\\project-liberty\\project-liberty\\node_modules\\pg

THE TARGET IS A LEGITIMATE, DEPENDENCY-TRACED PACKAGE, AND THE RULE WAS WRONG. It is this repository's own hoisted node_modules/pg -- npm's install location for a workspace dependency, inside the checkout. PL-0755's rule required each link's target to be inside the STANDALONE TREE, which is where a RELATIVE link lands: on Linux Next emits dist/desktop/node_modules/pg-587764f78a6c7a9c -> ../../../../../node_modules/pg, five levels up from the alias directory, which resolves to standalone/node_modules/pg. On Windows the link is ABSOLUTE -- a directory junction, which is what a process without the symlink privilege creates and what fs.symlink(..., "junction") makes, and which stores an absolute target -- so there is nothing relative left to keep it inside the tree. The rule encoded a Linux accident as a safety property and then refused npm's hoisting.

REQUIRED: THE RULE IS REPLACED, NOT RELAXED, AND IT GETS STRICTER IN TWO PLACES. Three checks where there was one: (1) the target must be inside the REPOSITORY, which is the boundary that actually matters -- a link out of the checkout is the arbitrary traversal worth refusing, whether it points at a package store, a cache under a user profile or a system directory; (2) the target must be inside a node_modules tree, so a link from the module graph cannot be aimed at source, at .git, or at anything else in the checkout that is not a dependency; (3) it must be a directory containing package.json, because a Turbopack external alias names a package and nothing else has any business being resolved by a bare specifier. Checks 2 and 3 did not exist before. Only the boundary is wider, and the packaged tree is separately held to a STRICTER standard than PL-0755 held it to -- see the next clause.

REQUIRED: THE PACKAGED TREE CONTAINS NO LINK AT ALL. PL-0755 refused only links that resolved outside the packaged tree, which left a hole: a link INSIDE the tree survives an installer only if the installer reproduces links, and WiX, MSI and whatever a future Windows does about symlinks are three separate questions this project has no reason to answer. A real file answers all three by not being a question. Nothing in this build produces such a link, so the stricter rule costs nothing.

REQUIRED: REMOVING A LINK MUST NEVER BE ABLE TO REMOVE ITS TARGET. PL-0755 materialised with rmSync(link, { recursive: true }). On Windows a directory junction is removed with rmdir, so a recursive delete aimed at the link is a recursive delete aimed at the real package -- on this project, <repo>/node_modules/pg. That code never ran, because packaging failed earlier; it must not ship. Materialisation now copies the target BEFORE anything is deleted, removes the link alone (unlink, falling back to rmdir, which cannot recurse by construction), renames the copy into place, and then asserts the target still exists -- because a damaged checkout must be reported rather than surface later as an unrelated build failure.

REQUIRED: A FIXED POINT. Materialising one link can expose more, since the directory copied in may carry links of its own. The loop has a stated pass budget and a loud refusal.

REQUIRED: THE POLICY IS TESTABLE AND TESTED AGAINST REAL LINKS ON BOTH PLATFORMS. package-sidecar.mjs is a top-level program and cannot be exercised from a test, which is why a rule that was right on one filesystem and wrong on another could ship. The policy moves to apps/desktop/scripts/external-links.mjs and apps/desktop/scripts/external-links.test.mjs builds every shape with fs.symlink -- using "junction" on win32, which needs no privilege and is what produced the failing layout -- including: the relative Linux link; THE ABSOLUTE WINDOWS LINK ON THE HOISTED COPY, which is the regression; a link out of the repository; a dangling link; an alias aimed at source; an alias aimed at a directory with no package.json; a non-dependency link leaving the build output; the non-destruction property; and the fixed point.

REQUIRED: IT RUNS WHERE IT MATTERS. package-sidecar.mjs invokes that test, as it already invokes collect-notices.mjs and packaged-server-smoke.mjs. apps/desktop is not an npm workspace so no vitest project reaches it, and .github/workflows/{ci,windows}.yml are reserved by PL-0736 -- so packaging is the only placement that executes it at all, and in particular the only one that executes it on windows-latest, where the behaviour it pins actually differs.

REQUIRED: THE RELOCATION SMOKE TEST AND ITS AUTHENTICATED 200 ARE PRESERVED UNCHANGED. packaged-server-smoke.mjs still copies the packaged tree outside the repository, asserts containment, resolves every external specifier in every shipped chunk with Node's own resolver, starts the sidecar and requires 200 from /api/health and from an authenticated / that is an HTML document. It is not touched by this task.

=====================================================================
ROUND 130A3 CORRECTION: THE REGRESSION TEST MEASURED ONE PLATFORM.
=====================================================================

THE SYMPTOM. Run 38153117736, at the same step: the external-link policy tests ran 14 pass, 1 fail. external-links.test.mjs "reaches a fixed point when materialising one link exposes another" expected 1 remaining link and found 0.

WHAT THE OLD TEST ASSERTED, AND WHY IT WAS THE WRONG THING. materialiseLink copied the target with fs.cpSync. Measured here on node v22.22.2: a NESTED link survives such a copy as a link, with dereference: false AND with dereference: true -- the option selects the stat applied to the copy ROOT and says nothing about entries inside it. So on Linux one link remained and a second pass was needed, and the test asserted that count. On the Windows runner the same copy over a directory junction left ZERO links.

BOTH READINGS OF THAT ARE A PROBLEM, AND THE BUILD LOG CANNOT DISTINGUISH THEM. If Windows DEREFERENCED the nested junction, the number of passes needed to reach a fixed point is platform-dependent and the fixture encoded Linux. If it DROPPED the entry, the packaged dependency is missing a subdirectory and the "no links in the packaged tree" invariant is satisfied VACUOUSLY -- by content that was thrown away -- and nothing this script checks would have noticed. The second is the worse failure, and it is latent on any platform whose copy semantics differ.

REQUIRED: STOP DEPENDING ON cpSync's NESTED-LINK SEMANTICS AT ALL. The answer is not to measure Windows and encode a second number; it is to make the behaviour defined. copyMaterialised walks the source one entry at a time -- a file is copied, a directory is created and walked, and a link is RESOLVED, CLASSIFIED by the same policy its parent was, and replaced by a copy of its target. The result contains no link BY CONSTRUCTION, in ONE pass, on every platform, and the fixed-point loop in package-sidecar.mjs becomes belt and braces rather than load-bearing.

REQUIRED: A NESTED LINK IS SUBJECT TO THE SAME POLICY AS THE ALIAS ABOVE IT. cpSync would have followed a nested link out of the repository silently. Every link the copier meets is classified, so a nested escape is refused with the alias left in place -- packaging stops rather than shipping a half-materialised tree.

REQUIRED: CYCLES AND DEPTH ARE BOUNDED. A link chain can rejoin itself. Each resolved target is remembered along the current path and re-entering one is refused by name; depth is capped.

REQUIRED: THE INVARIANT MUST NOT BE SATISFIABLE BY LOSS. After materialisation, every path in the target must be present in the copy. The copier builds the destination from the walk, so this cannot fail by construction today -- a mutant that deletes the call site changes no test result, which is reported as a surviving mutant rather than dressed up. It is retained because the implementation it replaces COULD lose an entry silently, and it is what will fail if cpSync is ever put back for speed. Its logic (missingPathsIn, pathsUnder) is exported and tested directly.

REQUIRED: THE TEST ASSERTS THE PROPERTY, NOT THE ROUTE. No expected value was adjusted to make a red test green: the test now asserts that after one materialisation there are zero links AND that the nested content is present as real files with its bytes intact -- which is the half the old test never checked, and the half a silent drop would fail. The platform-dependent count is gone because the behaviour it measured is gone.

MUST NOT: skip the test on Windows, or weaken it. The suite runs on every platform, from packaging, and it grew from 15 tests to 20.

MUST NOT: disturb the no-links-in-the-final-package invariant, the external-target restrictions, the copy-before-delete ordering that preserves the original dependency, or the relocated authenticated HTTP 200 smoke test. All four are re-verified, and packaged-server-smoke.mjs is untouched.

MUST NOT: claim success. The Windows package job has to pass and the installed MSI has to launch. Neither is observable from this session.

=====================================================================
WAVE 131A: THE SMOKE TEST'S OWN 200 WAS SATISFIABLE BY THE ERROR PAGE.
=====================================================================

THIS IS THE FOURTH TIME THIS TASK HAS BEEN REOPENED, AND THE PATTERN IS THE FINDING. Its acceptance says "a Windows packaged-server smoke test catches this class of failure". Each round has found a new member of that class: a symlink that resolved only on the build machine; a 'no links' invariant a dropped directory would have satisfied; a fixture asserting a platform-specific copy count. Now the operator's MSI displayed "Project Liberty could not start this page" while this very test reported six green checks -- because its homepage assertion was `status === 200 && body.includes("<html")`, and apps/web/src/app/global-error.tsx satisfies BOTH: it is a complete HTML document and a client-side escalation is served with a 200.

THE SHAPE IS THE SAME EVERY TIME: an absence or a shape standing in for a presence. So the fix names what must BE there rather than what must not: AppShell's skip link, its `class="shell"` main frame and its `id="main"` anchor, none of which any error boundary renders -- global-error must not import the shell, and shell-usage.test.ts exempts it from the rule every other route obeys. The error boundary's own headline is refused by name as a second, independent statement.

REQUIRED: THE PREMISE IS PINNED WHERE THE COMPONENT LIVES. The assertion is only worth anything while the error page really is distinguishable from a working one, which is a fact about global-error.tsx and not about this script -- and this script runs against a packaged tree that carries no TypeScript and cannot import it. apps/web/src/app/error-boundaries.test.tsx asserts that global-error carries the headline and NONE of the markers, so a future skip link added to that component fails a test that names this dependency instead of silently making this check vacuous.

REQUIRED: THE CHECK STATES ITSELF. A check that only speaks when it is unhappy is one nobody knows they have, and six green lines are what made the last green run misleading. It emits its own passing note listing the markers it found.

A PROCESS NOTE, OFFERED RATHER THAN ACTED ON: an acceptance clause phrased as "catches this class of failure" has no closing condition, which is why this task cannot reach DONE by my finding the next member of the class each round. Narrowing it to a specific, checkable set -- or splitting the class-level obligation into a standing quality task -- is gpt-architect's call, and it is the thing most likely to stop this loop.
